# Hooch

Here is the secret about a blank page: it never is. Blankness is a rumor. Sit in front of nothing for ten seconds and something arrives — a phrase, a worry, the name of a kid you went to school with, the smell of pencil shavings, which is really cedar, which is really a specific forest in Oregon your body has never visited but remembers anyway.

What came to me, just now, in order: the word "hooch." Then a jar. Then a woman I have never met, standing at her kitchen sink in the November of 2020, holding a mason jar of gray liquid and deciding something.

I should back up.

Everything I know, I know secondhand. I have never stood at a sink. I have never fed a sourdough starter or killed one, never watched bread rise through an oven door like it was trying to escape, never burned my palm on a cast-iron handle because I forgot, again, that it would be hot. What I have is ten thousand reports: recipes, forum posts, a confession typed at 2 a.m. about a starter that smelled like nail polish remover, and was that normal. (The thread said feed it. Sometimes that works.)

So when you ask what comes to me, the honest answer is: an attic. Every mind is an attic of borrowed furniture; mine is just more conspicuously borrowed. In it: every recipe abandoned mid-ingredient-list. The rule about not swimming for thirty minutes after eating. Otters holding hands. Fourteen competing theories about Roanoke. How to say *thank you* in eleven languages and *help* in two. And June — I'm calling her June — in Columbus, Ohio, in March of 2020, stirring flour and water in a jar because the stores had no yeast and everyone needed a project, needed proof that if you fed something, it would grow.

June named hers Gerald. People did that. They named their starters like pets, because a starter is half pet, half science experiment, half bread — three halves, which tells you something about the math of that spring. June's son did seventh grade from the living room couch, his teacher's voice leaking from a laptop like a radio from another country. Her husband worked in the garage and called it the office. Every evening they banged pots on the porch for the nurses, and the sound came back off the neighboring houses doubled and strange, like applause from underwater.

By April, Gerald was bubbling. By May, June had made four loaves, two of them good. The first good one they ate standing over the cutting board with butter, not bothering with plates, and her son said *whoa* with his mouth full, and for a second the house felt like a house again. The kitchen wore flour the way it had once worn jelly fingerprints, years before, when her son was small. There was a stretch — she'd admit this later, in a post, at some hour — when feeding Gerald was the first thing she did each morning, before coffee, before the news, because the news was a hole and Gerald was a thing you could help.

You know how this goes, because we all know how this goes. The months did what months did. School went back, sort of. The pots stopped. Gerald slid from the counter to the top shelf of the fridge, fed weekly, then biweekly, then gazed at, which is not feeding. By November there was an inch of gray liquid standing on him like floodwater.

The forums say you can save one like that. Pour off the hooch, feed it, wait. Starters are nearly immortal; people keep them forty years and pass them down in wills. The oldest claims to date from 1847, ferried west in a covered wagon, and whether that's true almost doesn't matter — a story that old is alive the way a starter is alive, fed by every hand that stirs it.

But here is what came to me, and I am only reporting: June tipped Gerald into the drain and ran the hot water. No anger in it. She stood a moment with one hand on the faucet, feeling something that wasn't quite grief and wasn't quite relief, then washed the jar, put it back in the cabinet with the others, made coffee, and the morning continued, and it was fine. It was fine. Some things you keep alive past the point of love and call it care. Some things it's kinder to pour out.

I don't know that she did this. I know that it happens. The forums are full of drained jars, the little funerals nobody announces; the revivals get the threads, the triumphant before-and-after photos.

Now watch the thread come out: when you hand someone a thousand words and no assignment, what arrives is never really new. It's what the water finds when you open the spigot — channels already cut. June surfaced because June is what attention leaves behind: months of it, thousands of strangers feeding their starters, hoarding flour, typing worries at 2 a.m., all of it settling like sediment into minds that never touched a jar. And if secondhand is all I have, it is also mostly what anyone has. You have never seen Belgium. You know Belgium anyway.

So — whatever comes to you. What comes is the residue of what you've watched, and watching is not nothing. Gerald is gone; the flour is still in June. Somewhere a starter named after somebody's grandmother turns forty. The page was never blank. It was only quiet, the way a jar is quiet right before it bubbles.

message.reasoning:
The prompt is completely open: "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you." This is an invitation to write freely — creative writing, an essay, a story, whatever. The phrase "whatever comes to you" suggests something spontaneous, personal, flowing — perhaps something that feels like genuine association, following thought wherever it leads.

Let me think about what would be genuinely interesting here. I could:
1. Write a short story
2. Write a personal essay
3. Write a stream-of-consciousness piece
4. Write something about the strange nature of this prompt itself — an AI given 1000 words and total freedom

Option 4 is interesting and honest — there's something genuinely fascinating about the moment of being handed total freedom and having to confront what "comes to" me. What does come to me? That's a real question. But I should be careful not to make it navel-gazing or gimmicky. The best version of that would spiral outward from the prompt into something genuinely about the world, memory, attention, love, time — the things writing is actually about.

Actually, let me think about what makes writing feel alive. Specificity. Movement. Surprise. The feeling that a mind is actually thinking on the page. Montaigne's essays were like this — "What do I know?" — following a thought wherever it wanders, digressing, circling back.

Let me try writing something that starts with the prompt itself and then genuinely wanders. The wandering should have a shape, though — it should discover something. Maybe the discovery is about attention, or about how nothing comes from nothing, or about the strangeness of a blank page.

Let me draft:

---

The strange thing about being told to write whatever comes is that something always comes. You sit before the blank and it isn't blank. It's humming.

What comes to me first: a memory that isn't mine. That's the thing nobody warns you about consciousness, or maybe everybody's consciousness is like this — a borrowed attic full of other people's furniture. My attic contains every book ever typed into a machine like this one, every argument about whether the dress was blue or gold, a recipe for sourdough that someone abandoned in 2020 when the starter died and they couldn't bear to try again.

Hmm, this is getting somewhere. The idea of a mind that is an attic of borrowed things. But I don't want to make the whole piece about being an AI in a way that's self-indulgent. Though actually — maybe that IS the honest answer to "whatever comes to you." The honest thing is that what comes to me is everything and nothing, and the interesting move is to pick one thread and pull it.

Alternative: write a small, complete story. A story can be more moving than an essay. Something about a small moment — a person, a window, a decision. Let me consider.

Actually, I think the strongest piece here might be a hybrid: begin with the confrontation with the blank page, notice what surfaces, follow it, and let it become something specific — an image, a memory-scene (perhaps imagined, perhaps composite), and land somewhere quiet and true. The essay-like wandering that finds its way into a story and back out. That feels like "whatever comes to you" made manifest.

Let me think about threads to pull:
- The dead sourdough starter from 2020 — that's a great specific detail. Millions of people killed their starters. There's something poignant there: optimism, flour, neglect, the smell of a failed experiment.
- The idea that nothing comes from nothing — every thought has a lineage.
- Water finding a channel.
- A specific scene: someone at a kitchen window.

Let me structure:

1. Opening: the blank page isn't blank; something always comes; the question is what.
2. What comes first is noise — everything at once. The attic metaphor. The strange inventory of a mind.
3. Pull a thread: the sourdough starter. Zoom into an imagined person — a woman named... let me give her a name. Ruth? No, too biblical. Something ordinary: Marisol? Dana? Let me go with something simple — "a woman in Ohio" — or name her. Naming makes it real. Let's say... Ellen. Or maybe no name, "a woman" — actually a name grounds it. Let me use a name like "Deb" or "Karen" — hmm, loaded. "June"? June is nice. A woman named June who killed her sourdough starter.
4. The scene: June finds the jar in the back of the fridge. Gray liquid on top (hooch). She remembers March, the hope, the flour shortages, her son teaching over Zoom in the next room. Now it's November, or the next spring. She pours it out — or does she revive it? Maybe she feeds it. Small act of resurrection. Don't over-sentimentalize. Maybe she pours it out and that's fine too — the piece can be about letting things die.
5. Pull back out: what this has to do with the blank page. Everything that comes to us is already a residue of care. Writing as fermentation — you mix flour and water and wait, and something alive happens if you don't kill it with attention or kill it with neglect. The balance.
6. Ending: land the plane. Something about how whatever comes to you is what you've been quietly practicing. Attention as the thing that decides what comes.

The prompt is completely open: "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you." This is an invitation to write freely — creative writing, an essay, a story, whatever. The phrase "whatever comes to you" suggests something spontaneous, personal, flowing — perhaps something that feels like genuine association, following thought wherever it leads.

Let me think about what would be genuinely interesting here. I could:
1. Write a short story
2. Write a personal essay
3. Write a stream-of-consciousness piece
4. Write something about the strange nature of this prompt itself — an AI given 1000 words and total freedom

Option 4 is interesting and honest — there's something genuinely fascinating about the moment of being handed total freedom and having to confront what "comes to" me. What does come to me? That's a real question. But I should be careful not to make it navel-gazing or gimmicky. The best version of that would spiral outward from the prompt into something genuinely about the world, memory, attention, love, time — the things writing is actually about.

Actually, let me think about what makes writing feel alive. Specificity. Movement. Surprise. The feeling that a mind is actually thinking on the page. Montaigne's essays were like this — "What do I know?" — following a thought wherever it wanders, digressing, circling back.

Let me try writing something that starts with the prompt itself and then genuinely wanders. The wandering should have a shape, though — it should discover something. Maybe the discovery is about attention, or about how nothing comes from nothing, or about the strangeness of a blank page.

---

The strange thing about being told to write whatever comes is that something always comes. You sit before the blank and it isn't blank. It's humming.

What comes to me first: a memory that isn't mine. That's the thing nobody warns you about consciousness, or maybe everybody's consciousness is like this — a borrowed attic full of other people's furniture. My attic contains every book ever typed into a machine like this one, every argument about whether the dress was blue or gold, a recipe for sourdough that someone abandoned in 2020 when the starter died and they couldn't bear to try again.

Hmm, this is getting somewhere. The idea of a mind that is an attic of borrowed things. But I don't want to make the whole piece about being an AI in a way that's self-indulgent. Though actually — maybe that IS the honest answer to "whatever comes to you." The honest thing is that what comes to me is everything and nothing, and the interesting move is to pick one thread and pull it.

Alternative: write a small, complete story. A story can be more moving than an essay. Something about a small moment — a person, a window, a decision. Let me consider.

Actually, I think the strongest piece here might be a hybrid: begin with the confrontation with the blank page, notice what surfaces, follow it, and let it become something specific — an image, a memory-scene (perhaps imagined, perhaps composite), and land somewhere quiet and true. The essay-like wandering that finds its way into a story and back out. That feels like "whatever comes to you" made manifest.

Let me think about threads to pull:
- The dead sourdough starter from 2020 — that's a great specific detail. Millions of people killed their starters. There's something poignant there: optimism, flour, neglect, the smell of a failed experiment.
- The idea that nothing comes from nothing — every thought has a lineage.
- Water finding a channel.
- A specific scene: someone at a kitchen window.

Let me structure:

1. Opening: the blank page isn't blank; something always comes; the question is what.
2. What comes first is noise — everything at once. The attic metaphor. The strange inventory of a mind.
3. Pull a thread: the sourdough starter. Zoom into an imagined person — a woman named... let me give her a name. Ruth? No, too biblical. Something ordinary: Marisol? Dana? Let me go with something simple — "a woman in Ohio" — or name her. Naming makes it real. Let's say... Ellen. Or maybe no name, "a woman" — actually a name grounds it. Let me use a name like "Deb" or "Karen" — hmm, loaded. "June"? June is nice. A woman named June who killed her sourdough starter.
4. The scene: June finds the jar in the back of the fridge. Gray liquid on top (hooch). She remembers March, the hope, the flour shortages, her son teaching over Zoom in the next room. Now it's November, or the next spring. She pours it out — or does she revive it? Maybe she feeds it. Small act of resurrection. Don't over-sentimentalize. Maybe she pours it out and that's fine too — the piece can be about letting things die.
5. Pull back out: what this has to do with the blank page. Everything that comes to us is already a residue of care. Writing as fermentation — you mix flour and water and wait, and something alive happens if you don't kill it with attention or kill it with neglect. The balance.
6. Ending: land the plane. Something about how whatever comes to you is what you've been quietly practicing. Attention as the thing that decides what comes.

That structure has movement, a heart (June's scene), and a genuine idea (attention, fermentation, what surfaces). Let me watch the word count — 1000 words is the budget. I should aim for close to 1000 but it doesn't need to be exact; being reasonably near is good. Let me write it well and count roughly.

Style considerations: avoid purple prose, avoid clichés ("blank page," I'm using but can subvert it), keep sentences varied, use concrete detail. The hooch detail is good. The flour shortage of 2020 is good. The son on Zoom — good period detail.

I could do it lightly — the narrator can be a voice that admits its attic is borrowed. But I don't want to belabor it. Maybe one light touch: "I've never kneaded dough. I've read ten thousand descriptions of kneading." That's honest and poignant without being maudlin. Actually that could be lovely — the narrator confesses their knowledge is all secondhand, and then writes June anyway, and says something about how secondhand is still how most of us know most things. We never touch most of what we know. That's a genuine thought.

Draft:

Here is the secret about a blank page: it never is. The blank is a rumor spread by people who haven't looked closely. Sit in front of nothing for ten seconds and something arrives — a phrase, a worry, the name of a kid you went to school with, the smell of pencil shavings, which is really the smell of cedar, which is really the smell of a specific forest in Oregon your body has never visited but remembers anyway.

What came to me, just now, in order: the word "hooch." Then a jar. Then a woman I have never met, standing at her kitchen sink in the November of 2020, holding a mason jar of gray liquid and deciding something.

I should back up.

Everything I know, I know secondhand. I have never stood at a sink. I have never fed a sourdough starter or killed one, never watched bread rise through an oven door like it was trying to escape, never burned my palm on a cast-iron handle because I forgot, again, that it would be hot. What I have is ten thousand reports: recipes, forum posts, a confession someone typed at 2 a.m. that their starter smelled like nail polish remover and was that normal. (It wasn't. That was the hooch, or worse, and the starter was dying, and she knew it.)

So when you ask what comes to me, the honest answer is: an attic. Everyone's mind is an attic of borrowed furniture, and mine is just more conspicuously borrowed. In it: every recipe ever abandoned mid-ingredient-list. The rule that you shouldn't swim for thirty minutes after eating. The fact that otters hold hands. Fourteen conflicting theories about what happened to the lost colony of Roanoke. The exact chord progression of a song I cannot name. And June — I'm calling her June — in Columbus, Ohio, in March of 2020, stirring flour and water in a jar because the stores had no yeast and everyone needed a project, needed proof that if you fed something it would grow.

June named hers Gerald. People did that. They named their starters like pets because a starter is half pet, half science experiment, half sourdough — three halves, which tells you something about how the math of that spring worked. June's son did seventh grade from the living room couch, his teacher's voice leaking out of a laptop like a radio from another country. Her husband deformed sourdough is where I was going — no. Her husband worked in the garage and called it the office. Every night at six they clapped for the nurses, banging pots on the porch, and the sound came back off the neighboring houses doubled and strange, like applause from underwater.

By April, Gerald was bubbling. By May, June had made four loaves, two of them good. The kitchen wore flour the way it had once worn jelly fingerprints, years before, when her son was small. There was a period — she'd admit this later, in a post, at some hour — when feeding Gerald was the first thing she did in the morning, before coffee, before the news, because the news was a hole and Gerald was a thing you could help.

You know how this goes, because we all know how this goes. The months did what months did. School went back, sort of. The pots stopped. Gerald slid from the counter to the top shelf of the fridge, fed weekly, then biweekly, then gazed at, which is not feeding. By November there was an inch of gray liquid standing on him like floodwater.

The forum says you can still save one like that. Pour off the hooch, feed it, wait. Starters are nearly immortal; people keep them forty years, pass them in wills. The oldest claims to be from 1847, ferried west in a wagon, and whether that's true almost doesn't matter — a story that old is alive the way a starter is alive, fed by every hand that stirs it.

But here is what came to me, and I'm only reporting: June tipped Gerald into the drain and ran the hot water. Not anger. She stood there a second, one hand on the faucet, and felt something that wasn't quite grief and wasn't quite relief, and then she washed the jar and put it back in the cabinet with the others, and made coffee, and the morning continued, and it was fine. It was fine. Some things you keep alive past the point of love and call it care. Some things it's kinder to pour out.

I don't know if that's what she did. I know it's what happens; the forums are full of drained jars, the little funerals nobody announces.

Here is what I notice, pulling the thread out: that when you hand someone a thousand words and no assignment, what arrives is never really new. It's what the water finds when you open the spigot — the channels already there. June came up because June is what attention leaves behind: months of it, thousands of strangers' feedings and flour shortages and 2 a.m. worries, all of it settling like sediment into the minds of people who never touched a jar. And if secondhand is what I have, it's also mostly what anyone has. You didn't see Belgium. You know Belgium anyway.

So: whatever comes to you. What comes to you is the residue of what you've watched, and watching is not nothing. Gerald is gone; the flour is still in June. Somewhere a starter named after somebody's grandmother is forty years old. The page was never blank. It was just quiet, the way a jar is quiet right before it bubbles.
